ranked.title: Burning solids release CO - detect gases, not only smoke
ranked.finding: In 118 BASS-II tests (small solid samples in the ISS glovebox) CO rose by a median 45 ppm, 90th percentile 413 ppm, maximum 575 ppm per test.
ranked.action: Pair smoke detection with CO (and CO2) sensing in crew volumes; toxic gas, not heat, killed the Apollo 1 crew.

ranked.title: Less oxygen makes flames go out earlier
ranked.finding: Lowering O2 from 21 % to 15 % changes the droplet size at flame extinction (relative to the initial size) by +50 % (95 % CI +34 % to +79 %; 188 FLEX tests with extinction): more fuel is left unburned.
ranked.action: Reducing O2 (venting, inert flooding) is an effective way to shorten a microgravity fire.
sources: NASA PSI-69 FLEX Experimental Table (https://psi.nasa.gov), NASA/TP-2015-216046

ranked.title: More oxygen burns fuel faster
ranked.finding: Raising O2 from 21 % to 30 % (other conditions fixed) changes the droplet burning rate by +44 % (95 % CI +39 % to +55 %), from 257 FLEX tests on the ISS.
ranked.action: Treat every percent of extra O2 in a habitat as a fire-hazard increase; tighten material screening and ignition-source control when O2 is raised above sea-level air.
sources: NASA PSI-69 FLEX Experimental Table (https://psi.nasa.gov), NASA/TP-2015-216046

ranked.title: At 30 % O2 droplet flames rarely put themselves out
ranked.finding: N2-diluted FLEX tests: the flame burned the droplet out without extinguishing in 54 % of 13 tests at O2 >= 30 %, vs 14 % of 58 tests at O2 <= 21 %.
ranked.action: At elevated O2 assume a fire will not self-extinguish; active suppression must be immediate.
sources: NASA PSI-69 FLEX Experimental Table (https://psi.nasa.gov), NASA/TP-2015-216046

ranked.title: In O2-rich streams gaseous fuels ignite almost every time
ranked.finding: ACME CFI-G inverse flames on the ISS: ignition in 98 % of 101 attempts with oxidizer O2 >= 50 % (up to 85 %), vs 67 % of 33 attempts below 30 %.
ranked.action: Treat O2 lines, regulators and O2-generator outlets as top-priority ignition hazards (keep hydrocarbons and electrical heat sources away from them).
sources: NASA PSI-159 ACME CFI-G Experimental Tables (https://psi.nasa.gov)

ranked.title: Helium dilution does not slow burning - it speeds it up
ranked.finding: Replacing 30 % of the nitrogen by helium changes the burning rate by +35 % (95 % CI +30 % to +42 %; 257 FLEX tests): helium conducts heat to the droplet faster.
ranked.action: Helium is not a substitute for CO2 as a fire-suppressing diluent; account for it if He is used as a cabin diluent.
sources: NASA PSI-69 FLEX Experimental Table (https://psi.nasa.gov), NASA/TP-2015-216046

ranked.title: A Moon-base atmosphere burns droplets faster than ISS air
ranked.finding: Hybrid model, 3 mm droplet: Moon-base atmosphere (O2 30 %, 10.2 psi) vs ISS cabin air (O2 21 %, 1 atm): methanol +32 % (95 % band -2 % to +77 %); heptane +32 % (95 % band -2 % to +79 %). Label: extrapolation (O2 30 % was tested only from 0.703 atm).
ranked.action: Size fire-detection response and suppression capacity of Moon-base modules and rovers for faster fuel consumption than on the ISS; re-test cabin materials at the planned atmosphere.

ranked.title: CO2 dilution slows burning
ranked.finding: Replacing 30 % of the nitrogen by CO2 (same O2 and pressure) changes the burning rate by -7 % (95 % CI -11 % to -3 %; 257 FLEX tests).
ranked.action: CO2 is an effective diluent suppressant in microgravity; keep it in the suppression design.
sources: NASA PSI-69 FLEX Experimental Table (https://psi.nasa.gov), NASA/TP-2015-216046

ranked.title: Lowering cabin pressure barely slows burning
ranked.finding: Going from 1.0 to 0.7 atm at the same O2 fraction changes the burning rate by -3 % (95 % CI -7 % to +0 %; 257 FLEX tests).
ranked.action: Do not count on reduced habitat pressure to offset the added hazard of a higher O2 fraction.
sources: NASA PSI-69 FLEX Experimental Table (https://psi.nasa.gov), NASA/TP-2015-216046

ranked.title: Smoke from spacecraft materials has been measured in microgravity
ranked.finding: SAME-R ran 109 smoke tests on the ISS with 5 materials (Kapton, Lampwick, Pyrell, Silicone, Teflon) - the data base for smoke detectors tuned to microgravity smoke.
ranked.action: Use SAME/SAME-R particle data when specifying detectors for new spacecraft rather than terrestrial detector standards.

ranked.title: Cool flames: fuel can keep reacting after the visible flame is gone
ranked.finding: Cool flames were recorded in 8 of 179 ACME CFI-G normal-flame tests; FLEX test notes report cool-flame burning after visible-flame extinction of heptane droplets (NASA/TP-2015-216046).
ranked.action: Do not declare a fire out on optical (visible/UV flame) evidence alone; confirm with gas sensing and temperature.

ranked.title: On the lunar surface a droplet burns between its ISS and Earth rates
ranked.finding: Moon-base air (O2 0.30, 10.2 psi), 3 mm droplet at 1/6 g: the burning rate lies between the microgravity rate and 1.46x (methanol) / 1.44x (heptane) that rate (Law & Williams buoyancy correction, Gr = 0.76 / 0.69, inside its fitted range Gr <= 1). Lower bound = microgravity; no partial-gravity data in PSI.
ranked.action: Size Moon-base fire response for a burning rate up to the upper bound, and treat ISS-derived burn times as the slow limit.
sources: Law & Williams, Combust. Flame 19 (1972) Eq. (9); docs/PHYSICS.md section 4

ranked.title: NASA: for solid materials, lunar gravity may be the most flammable condition
ranked.finding: NASA Glenn reports that "Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition" for solid materials (flame spread peaks and the oxygen limit is lowest near lunar g), and a partial-g habitat fire is expected to be "substantially worse than in 0-g and potentially worse than even 1-g". The FM2 experiment is to measure this on the Moon.
ranked.action: Do not assume a material that passes the 1-g screening test is safe in a Moon base; add margin until lunar data (FM2) exist.
sources: NTRS 20210020516 (Fire on the Moon, NASA GRC)

ranked.title: Without buoyancy the same droplet burns slower than on Earth
ranked.finding: Law & Williams buoyancy correction for a 3 mm droplet in air at 1 atm: Earth burning rate is 3.0x (methanol) and 2.9x (heptane) the microgravity rate (correlation used far outside its fitted range, Gr = 13).
ranked.action: Do not transfer Earth flammability or detection-time results to spacecraft without microgravity data; microgravity flames are smaller and slower, so they may be detected later.
sources: Law & Williams, Combust. Flame 19 (1972) Eq. (9); docs/PHYSICS.md section 4

history_and_earth.title: Apollo 1: pure oxygen turned a spark into a flash fire
history_and_earth.finding: "Because of the pure oxygen atmosphere, the fire spread quickly"; the crew died of "asphyxia from carbon monoxide and other toxic gases" (NASA SMA).
history_and_earth.action: Our data show the same physics at milder O2 levels (P1, S4) and the CO hazard (D1).

history_and_earth.title: Apollo 13: oxygen system plus electrical heat
history_and_earth.finding: Heaters in the oxygen tank overheated, "degrading the Teflon insulation"; the redesign sheathed wiring "in stainless steel" (NASA SMA).
history_and_earth.action: O2-rich hardware is where ignition-source control matters most (P4).

history_and_earth.title: Mir 1997: a real fire in microgravity
history_and_earth.finding: An oxygen generator burned; "The flame blocked the evacuation route to the Soyuz spacecraft"; smoke was cleared "over several hours" (NASA History).
history_and_earth.action: Microgravity fires produce lasting smoke and gases (D1, D2) and can cut off escape routes: detection and immediate suppression (S3) are critical.

history_and_earth.title: Lighter firefighter air tanks
history_and_earth.finding: Developed with NASA Johnson Space Center: "20 pounds for 30 minute air supply" (NASA Spinoff, 1976).
history_and_earth.action: Benefit on Earth of NASA life-support work.

history_and_earth.title: Incipient fire detector from the Space Shuttle
history_and_earth.finding: Signals fire "before appearance of flame and smoke" and is "less susceptible to false alarms" (NASA Spinoff, 1978).
history_and_earth.action: Space detection technology already protects mines and buildings; SAME data (D3) can do the same.

history_and_earth.title: Fire-resistant gear from Apollo materials
history_and_earth.finding: Project FIRES used "lightweight, fire-resistant, heat-protective materials" from space suits (NASA Spinoff, 1982).
history_and_earth.action: Materials screened for O2-rich cabins protect firefighters on Earth.
